title: Exchange Connectivity, Sessions and Reconciliation
objectives: Describe the session lifecycle: logon, sequence negotiation, heartbeats, logout and day rollover
Detect a dead or stalled session and recover with resend or snapshot strategies
Explain replay semantics and why re-apply must be idempotent
Reconcile firm records against venue statements and classify breaks
motivation: Networks fail on a schedule nobody controls: a switch reboots, a venue pauses multicast, a WAN link flaps. The desk's protection is not luck, it is session discipline: heartbeats that detect silence, sequence numbers that measure exactly what was missed, replay that recovers it, and end-of-day reconciliation that proves the firm's books match the venue's.

blocks.text: A session is also a state machine

blocks.md: Order and market-data sessions are state machines layered on TCP: **logon** (authenticate, agree a heartbeat interval, and agree whether sequence numbers reset), **established** (messages flow under monotonic sequence numbers), **logout**, and **day rollover**, most venues reset sequences at the start of the trading day, and yesterday's numbers mean nothing today. Both sides remember 'the last sequence I sent / received'; that shared memory is what makes recovery cheap and exact.

A quiet session is not a healthy session. TCP will happily stay half-dead. Sessions therefore exchange **heartbeats** every few seconds (venues commonly use intervals of 10-30 seconds; the exact value is negotiated at logon). If no message, data or heartbeat, arrives within roughly one to two intervals, the client sends a **test request** demanding an immediate heartbeat; if that also goes unanswered, the session is declared dead and re-established. The expensive part is not the reconnect, it is every order quoted in the dark while the link was silently gone.

blocks.title: Quote guard
blocks.md: Serious desks gate order flow on session health: if the order session or the data feed is suspect, pull quotes first and debug second. Reconnecting is routine; trading blind is the incident.

On reconnect the client says 'I processed up to sequence $s$', and the venue resends from $s + 1$. For small gaps that resend is the whole fix. For large gaps, or market data, where a full book is cheaper to reload than to replay, load a **snapshot**, note its sequence, then re-apply live deltas newer than it. Two disciplines make replay safe: **idempotency** (re-applied fills must not double-count; key on execution and order IDs) and **ordering** (park live messages until the backfill finishes).

blocks.title: Sizing a replay
items: You last processed sequence 1,205; on reconnect the venue reports its last sent sequence is 1,260.
At roughly 150 bytes each: $55 \times 150 = 8{,}250$ bytes, trivial bandwidth, but the *book* is wrong until all 55 are applied.
The fix is bounded and fast only because the gap was detected instantly, which is what sequence numbers are for.

blocks.md: Every evening the firm's capture log is compared against the venue's official records, fills, positions, cash. Mismatches are **breaks**, and each one is a story: a fill missed during a disconnect, a duplicate applied, a sign flipped, a symbol mapped wrong. Venues also run a **drop copy**, an independent, read-only feed of the firm's orders sent straight to the risk system, so risk sees what actually reached the market even if the primary session or OMS is compromised.

Two breaks, 150 shares in total, must be explained before the next session. Breaks are not 'adjusted away', they are investigated until the cause is named, because an unexplained break means either the firm's ledger or the venue's is wrong, and you do not yet know which.

guidedExercise.prompt: You last processed sequence 500. On reconnect the venue reports last sent $= 640$. (a) How many messages will be replayed? (b) If each averages 200 bytes, how many bytes arrive? (c) Your book already applied everything up to 500, what two properties must your re-apply logic have?
hints: Replay covers everything after the last processed sequence.
Resends can repeat messages you already hold; think dedupe and ordering.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $640 - 500 = 140$ messages (sequences 501-640). (b) $140 \times 200 = 28{,}000$ bytes. (c) **Idempotency**, if the replay overlaps anything already applied, execution/order IDs must dedupe it, and **ordering**, live messages arriving during the replay are parked until the backfill completes.

independentExercise.prompt: Reconcile four symbols (ours vs venue): ABC +1,000 vs +1,000; BBB -400 vs -350; CCC +250 vs +250; DDD 0 vs -150. (a) Which symbols break? (b) What is the total absolute break size in shares? (c) For BBB, which direction does the investigation go: a fill we missed, or a duplicate we applied?
hints: A break is the difference between the two ledgers.
The venue shows more selling than we captured on BBB, what does that suggest?
independentExercise.solution: (a) BBB and DDD. (b) BBB: $|-400 - (-350)| = 50$; DDD: $|0 - (-150)| = 150$; total $200$ shares. (c) BBB: the venue shows 50 more sold than we captured, consistent with a sell fill missed during a disconnect; replay that session and look for the missing execution report before assuming an error on either side.

commonMistakes: Treating 'TCP is connected' as 'the session is healthy', only heartbeats and sequence flow prove liveness.
Re-applying replayed fills without ID dedupe, positions and PnL double-count.
Resetting sequence numbers mid-day without both sides agreeing, recovery then returns the wrong messages.
Adjusting the book to match the venue statement instead of finding the break's cause.
realWorldApplication: FIX session protocol implementations, open-source and proprietary, run exactly this machinery on every desk, and exchange onboarding tests verify heartbeat, resend and reconciliation behaviour before a firm may trade.
quantFinanceApplication: PnL is only credible if positions reconcile; quant research replaying a trading day needs gap-free, deduplicated session logs, the artifacts this discipline produces.
summary: Sessions: logon (credentials, heartbeat, sequence policy) -> established -> logout; sequences reset on day rollover by agreement.
Heartbeats and test requests convert silent failure into a detectable event within seconds (intervals commonly 10-30 s, negotiated).
Recovery: small gap -> resend from last sequence + 1; large gap -> snapshot, then re-apply newer deltas; always idempotent.
End-of-day reconciliation compares capture log vs venue ledger; breaks are root-caused, never adjusted; drop copies give risk an independent view.

quiz.prompt: On reconnect you find a small sequence gap. What is the best response?
options: Request a resend of the missing sequence range
Ignore the gap and continue with live messages
quiz.explanation: Small gaps are exactly what resend requests exist for; ignoring the gap corrupts the book, and a restart is a far bigger hammer than needed.

quiz.prompt: You last processed sequence 3,300. On reconnect the venue reports its last sent sequence is 3,352. How many messages must be replayed?
Which of these are part of sound session management?
options: Negotiate the heartbeat interval at logon
Resume from the last processed sequence number
Make re-applied replays idempotent with ID dedupe
Keep quoting while the session is suspect
quiz.explanation: Heartbeats, sequence resumption and idempotent replay are the discipline. Quoting on a suspect session is how desks trade against a dead market.

quiz.prompt: At reconciliation your ledger shows a flat position in XYZ but the venue statement shows short 300. What is the break size (absolute)?
quiz.explanation: $|0 - (-300)| = 300$ shares, every break needs a named cause, such as a missed sell fill during a disconnect.

quiz.prompt: What is a drop copy and why do firms want one?
quiz.modelAnswer: A drop copy is an independent, read-only feed of the firm's orders sent directly to the risk system, so risk can verify what actually reached the venue even if the primary session or OMS is broken, a last-line input for kill-switch decisions.
quiz.explanation: It is independence that matters: the copy travels a different path than the trading session, so a compromised session cannot hide what it sent.

quiz.prompt: The negotiated heartbeat interval is 10 s (illustrative). No message of any kind has arrived for 22 s. Best next action?
options: Wait another 10 s. TCP will recover by itself
Send a test request demanding an immediate heartbeat, and treat further silence as a dead session
Send a new order to test the link
Log off gracefully and go home
quiz.explanation: 22 s is beyond two intervals: send a test request now. If it goes unanswered, the session is dead, reconnect and resume from the last sequence. Testing with orders is how desks accidentally trade on dead links.

flashcards.back: A periodic do-nothing message proving the session is alive; silence beyond ~1-2 intervals triggers a test request, then reconnect.
last sent, last processed = number of messages to replay (sequences lastProcessed+1 .. lastSent).
Small gap: retransmit the range. Large gap: load a snapshot at sequence S, then apply live deltas with sequence > S.
A mismatch between the firm's ledger and the venue's official record; it must be root-caused, not adjusted.
